# Defects register — gaps, bugs, and defects to fix in the rebuild

> **Living document.** Ian, 2026-08-23: *"these surfacing gaps, bugs and defects — document
> them so we can fix as we build this project."*
>
> ### A defect here is never an argument against the feature
> Bible §1.2b — every feature in a reference repo exists because the business needed it and
> uses it daily. **A flawed implementation is evidence of a real need, not a proposal to drop.**
> Log the defect, harvest the intent, build it correctly here. If a feature looks pointless,
> **ask Ian** — something in daily operations probably explains it.
>
> ### ⛔ Nothing here is fixed at the source
> All four reference repos — `ERP-rebuild`, `POS`, `CUSTOMER`, `Shareat Website` — are
> **read-only** (bible §2 rule 1, §13 row 80). Every entry below is fixed **in the rebuild**.
> A defect is logged here, its business rule is harvested, and the correct behaviour is built
> into Shareat System. We never patch the reference.

## How to use this

- **Add a row the moment a defect is found.** Cite `file:line`. An unlogged finding is a lost one.
- ⭐ **Including one you found in passing** (bible §13 row 164). If you tripped over it while
  reading v1 for something else entirely, it still gets a row before you move on. *"It wasn't my
  task"* is not a reason to skip it — you are the only person who will ever have that context.
- ⛔ **Is it actually a defect?** A **defect** is v1 doing something *wrong*. Something v1 does
  that **no phase of the rebuild owns** is a **gap**, and it belongs in
  [`CAPABILITY-GAPS.md`](./CAPABILITY-GAPS.md) instead — this register's dispositions cannot
  express *"nobody has this"*, so a gap filed here is a gap buried here. The capability-gap pass
  is what caught the five ledger-posting modules January needed.
- **Verified means *I* read the code**, not that an agent reported it. Agent findings are
  `reported` until checked — three of four explorers on 2026-08-23 made at least one claim that
  did not survive verification.
- When a rebuild task closes a defect, mark it and name the task.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Sev** | ⛔ correctness/money · ⚠️ structural risk · 🔸 quality/maintenance |
| **State** | `verified` (read the code) · `reported` (agent, unchecked) · `fixed` |
| **Disposition** | What the rebuild does about it |

⛔ **A claim that turns out to be false is RETRACTED IN PROSE AT THE HEAD OF ITS CELL, never deleted and never quietly edited away** — the original stays below a `THE ORIGINAL CLAIM, KEPT` marker so the reasoning that produced it remains inspectable. There is no `retracted` state; the State column describes the underlying defect, which may still be `fixed`. Used twice so far: DEF-326's disproven hypothesis (2026-09-13) and DEF-345's headline (2026-09-14). ⚠️ **Retraction goes FIRST in the cell**, because a reader who acts on a false headline has already acted by the time they reach a correction at the bottom.

---

Receipt number is UNIQUE per store by constraint, not convention |

Never one integer column pretending to be both. ADR-003 |

| **DEF-065** | ⛔ | ERP-rebuild | **A split expense funded twice from the SAME sub-account silently loses one leg's audit trail.** `expense.builder.ts:19-135` derives each split's `legKey` from the sub-account it routes to — `cash:cashier`, `cash:office`, `cash:staff`, `online:{accountId}` — and **not** from the split's array index. `buildJournalEntryId(sourceType, sourceId, legKey)` (`journal-writer.ts:89`) turns that into a deterministic document id, so two splits with the same legKey resolve to the SAME journal entry doc, and `t.set(p.entryRef, entryData)` (`journal-writer.ts:168`) makes the second write a literal overwrite inside one transaction. One split's amount survives in the ledger; the other's does not, while the account balance — maintained separately by `FieldValue.increment` — may still reflect both. ⚠️ **This is reachable through a sanctioned feature, not an edge case.** `liquidation.ts:36-48` explicitly documents and supports *“a single receipt split across MULTIPLE cash requests”*, and every cash-request-funded split produces the same `cash:staff` legKey regardless of which request funded it. Two cashier-cash rows, or two online rows against one account, collide the same way. ⭐ **The same file already knows the fix.** Its reimbursable branch uses `reimbursable:{staffId}:{idx}` and `salary-advance.builder.ts:116` uses `${legSuffix}:${idx}` — both index-suffixed precisely to avoid this. The omission is builder-specific, not systemic, which is why it survived. It matters here more than anywhere else: expense payment is **4,396 legs, ~88% of v1's ledger activity**, and split funding is one of its named variants. | `reported` | v2 does not inherit the shape: `expense_payments` is a real child table with one row per split and its own `id`, and `postEntry` writes lines under a single entry rather than one document per leg, so two splits to the same account are two rows and cannot overwrite each other. ⚠️ **What v2 must NOT copy is the legKey idea itself** — any future per-leg deterministic key must include the split's identity, not just its destination account. **Worth an empirical check before cutover:** how many v1 expenses carry two splits resolving to one sub-account? Those entries' journal legs are already wrong in the live books, and `reconcileAccounts()` would have logged the drift only if someone ran it. |
| **DEF-069** | ⚠️ | **Shareat System** | ⭐ **A hand-written migration whose journal `when` is EARLIER than the previous entry's is silently skipped — and `db:migrate` still prints “Migrations applied”.** `packages/db/migrations/meta/_journal.json`'s timestamps are **synthetic, exactly 86,400,000 ms apart**, and drizzle applies entries by `when > last applied`. Journalling a new migration with `Date.now()` — the obvious thing to do — produces a value **behind** the synthetic series (0026 carried `1788319907084`, roughly a week ahead of real time), so the migration is treated as already applied. ⛔ **Nothing fails.** The command exits 0, prints the same success line, and records nothing in `drizzle.__drizzle_migrations`. Caught on 0027 only because the table was probed directly afterwards; a `\dt` or an assumption would have missed it, and the first failure would have surfaced much later as a missing-relation error against a schema file that looked perfectly correct. | `fixed` | ⭐ **Journal a new migration as `previous.when + 86400000`, never `Date.now()`** — the series is a monotonic ordinal, not a clock. ⚠️ **And verify the migration landed by querying `information_schema`, never by trusting the exit code**, exactly as “Deploy complete!” is not readiness for a Firestore index. Both databases are checked here (`shareat_dev` and `shareat_test`), because a migration that reaches only one produces integration tests that pass against a schema the app does not have. |
| **DEF-070** | ⚠️ | ERP-rebuild (its OWN bucket — **not** shared) · ⏸️ **ACCEPTED, deferred by Ian 2026-08-27** | ⭐ **ANY SIGNED-IN USER CAN READ EVERY FILE IN THE STORAGE BUCKET — every store, every ORG.** `storage.rules:34-36` is `match /{allPaths=**} { allow read: if request.auth != null; }`. There is no store check and no org check, so a franchise owner signed into their own org can read another org's receipt photos, purchase proofs, memo documents and onboarding files. ⚠️ **Found while specifying T-141, in the rules file's own neighbourhood.** The block immediately below it documents a *narrower* hole honestly — *“any signed-in user can write into any store's folder”* — and that admission is what ADR-002 §3 set out to close. The READ rule above it is broader, undocumented, and was not on anyone's list. ⚠️ **CORRECTED 2026-08-27, and narrower than first registered.** I recorded this as sharing a bucket with POS and CUSTOMER. It does not: v1's ERP is alone in `studio-7300228488-a394e`, while POS and CUSTOMER share `shareat-hub-v2`. So the exposure is **across orgs inside the ERP**, and it never reached POS/CUSTOMER files or diners. The finding stands; its blast radius was overstated. ⭐ **And checking that turned up the more important fact**, now bible row 155: `shareat-hub-v2`'s bucket is `allow read;` — **no condition at all, world-readable** — which is correct for the menu photos it holds and is exactly why accounting documents must never go there. ⛔ **The asymmetry is the finding:** v2 spent T-120 putting franchise isolation into Postgres precisely because *“a franchise with a separate owner is already live (Padre Garcia)”* — RLS, `FORCE`, default-deny — while **the bytes describing those same books have no isolation at all**. A receipt photo is a business document; reading one is reading another owner's books by other means. | `verified` | ⭐ T-141 brokers reads as well as writes: no client touches the bucket, paths are derived server-side from the session, and reads go through a route that calls `authorize()` and mints a minutes-long signed URL. `storage.rules` then reduces to **deny-all**, which also removes the whole class of rules landmines this project has already recorded (OR-semantics, `firestore.get()` failing silently) — a rule you cannot get wrong beats one you have to get right. ⚠️ **Sequencing is the risk, not the code**: the bucket is shared with POS and CUSTOMER, which still write directly, and this project has already recorded a case of one repo's deploy overwriting another's ruleset. Tighten writes to the ERP service account first; deny-all last. ⏸️ **DEFERRED, and deliberately — Ian, 2026-08-27:** *“later when Shareat System is done we can touch the ruleset of the backend of v1, tighten or loosen what’s needed.”* ⭐ **This is a risk ACCEPTANCE with an end date, not a fix**, and it is the right call: v1 is live, its rules file is the one construct this project has repeatedly recorded as failing SILENTLY when edited wrong (`firestore.get()`, OR-semantics), and it cannot be verified from an Admin-SDK script because Admin bypasses rules. Editing it mid-cutover risks breaking a system being retired, to close a hole whose readers are franchise owners rather than the public. ⚠️ **What makes the acceptance safe is that v2 does not inherit it:** bible row 155 puts v2's documents in a NEW private bucket, so the exposure stops growing from today and ends when v1 does. ⛔ Revisit if v1's lifetime extends materially, or if a franchise relationship turns adversarial — the exposure is one owner reading another's supplier invoices, and that is a commercial secret, not just a privacy one. |
| **DEF-071** | ⛔ | ERP-rebuild | ⭐ **A MONTHLY OWNER DRAWING LIMIT IS SETTABLE, DISPLAYED ON SCREEN, AND NEVER ENFORCED.** `OwnerPlain.drawingLimitPeriod` is typed `'monthly' \| 'total' \| null` and the equity page writes either value (`app/accounting/equity/page.tsx:103`) and **renders it back to the user as a live constraint** — *“Drawing Limit (monthly) ₱50,000”* (`page.tsx:339-340`). But the only check in the whole repo is `equity.actions.ts:249`: `if (owner.drawingLimit && owner.drawingLimitPeriod === 'total')`. ⛔ **A `'monthly'` limit therefore falls through to no check at all** — the owner is shown a cap that does not exist, and a withdrawal of any size posts. ⚠️ **The failure mode is worse than an unenforced rule:** a displayed limit is a control people believe in and stop watching. `'total'` is enforced, which makes the omission look like an oversight in a code path someone was actively editing rather than a feature nobody finished. ⭐ Found while specifying T-127, by asking what enforces each field on the owner document. | `verified` | ⭐ T-127 enforces **both** periods, and enforces them **from the ledger** rather than from a stored total — the monthly window is a sum of `3200` for that owner within the calendar month, so the check cannot disagree with the drawings it is checking. ⚠️ The v1 check reads `owner.totalDrawings`, one of the three stored figures DEF-072 covers; a limit computed from a drifting total is a limit that fails in the direction of letting money out. |
| **DEF-075** | ⚠️ | ERP-rebuild | ⭐ **`ARCustomerPlain.outstandingBalance` — A STORED BALANCE BESIDE THE LEDGER, FOR THE FIFTH TIME** (`types/index.ts:1574`). | **DEF-076** | ⚠️ | ERP-rebuild | **`ap_open/{supplierId}/{expenseId}` is a hand-maintained Firestore projection that went stale in production.** `receiptId` was added to the projection write (`ap-projection.server.ts`) after the collection was already live, so every `ap_open` doc written before that change kept `receiptId: null` while the source `expense` doc had the correct value all along. The "Pay receipt" / "Credit Expense (Receipt)" flow (`ap-details-client.tsx`) groups and filters open items by `ap_open.receiptId`, so a receipt with 7 open items showed 1, with wrong totals — the projection, not the source document, was wrong. If a receipt-grouping feature is ever needed, group by `expenses.supplier_invoice_id` read from the source rows directly, never from a cached copy. |

Everything from 0020 on was hand-written, so drizzle's snapshot chain has been dead since 0019 and `db:generate` diffs the CURRENT schema against a seventeen-migration-old baseline. ⚠️ **It fails in the most misleading way available:** it opens an interactive prompt asking whether `useful_life_months` is a NEW column or a RENAME of `useful_life_years` — a question settled back in T-124, where the live database and the schema both already say `useful_life_months`. | **DEF-166** | ⚠️ | ERP-rebuild | **`voidSalesDayAction`'S DOC-COMMENT CLAIMS A SNAPSHOT/MONTH-INDEX CASCADE ITS CODE NEVER RUNS.** The docstring (`ERP-rebuild/src/lib/actions/sales-day.actions.ts:164-165`) states that voiding a sales day "removes it from the month index, and enqueues ledger/snapshot recompute." The function body (`167-309`) does neither: no month-index write for this collection exists anywhere in the repo (grepped repo-wide for "month index" — zero hits outside the comment), and there is no call to the `cascadeSnapshots` chain the sibling Sales Report Adjustment flow explicitly runs for an equivalent-size restatement. So a void and an adjustment of the same magnitude leave downstream rollups in different states, and the comment asserts the safer of the two. Found in passing 2026-09-04 during the Phase 6 reporting discovery pass (`docs/discovery/26-reporting-dashboards-and-insights.md` §A.1, §A.4) | `verified` — code read directly | **Structural in v2, not a port.** A sales-day void is `reverseEntry` inside one transaction (bible §4.2 rule 9), and every downstream figure is a live query over `journal_lines` (phase-6 plan §2), so there is no snapshot to cascade to and no month index to forget. Recorded so the *intent* — a void must trigger the same re-derivation an equivalent adjustment does — is preserved rather than assumed. Closed by T-209/T-210's read model; no separate fix task. |

When that transaction commits, PostgreSQL resets the GUC to `''` (empty string), **not** to unset/NULL — a documented quirk of custom GUCs that only ever had a `LOCAL` assignment, and exactly why `app_current_org()`'s `NULLIF(..., '')` guard exists at all. `principal.ts`'s own customer branch is the reachable path: *"Customer: NO org is set, so every org-scoped policy evaluates against NULL"* — true on a **fresh** connection, false on a **pooled, reused** one that previously served a staff request: `app.org_id` reads back `''`, not NULL. Reproduced live with a `max: 1` pool (forcing reuse): a staff transaction sets a real `org_id` and commits; the next transaction on the same connection, applying a customer principal exactly as `applyPrincipal` does, reads `current_setting('app.org_id', true)` as `''`; every table still on the raw idiom throws `22P02` where `app_current_org()`'s tables cleanly deny with zero rows. Verified independently twice — once by this row's author (superuser connection, which bypasses RLS via `rolbypassrls=true` and initially produced a false "not reachable" conclusion), then corrected by a peer session's second pass, which is the version above, itself re-verified live before writing this row. **Still not a data leak** — a policy-evaluation error still returns zero rows to the client, it just does it as a 500 instead of a clean empty result — but it is a **live, reachable, customer-facing availability defect**: any customer-kind request whose connection was previously used for a staff request will 500 on any of the ~10 affected tables, unpredictably, depending on pool reuse history. Found by a peer session's audit of T-130, mid-wrap-up; the reachability correction is from that same peer's second pass | `verified` | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-28 — all of it, both databases.** Migration `0044` DROP/CREATEs the six remaining policies (`customers`, `price_lists`, `price_list_items`, `liabilities`, `owners`, `owner_drawing_closes`) onto `app_current_org()`; T-130's own four were already done in `0043`. ⚠️ **The count in this row's description was wrong — it is SIX, not ~10**, confirmed by querying `pg_policies` on both databases rather than grepping migration text. Both now read **44 of 44 policies on `app_current_org()`, zero raw**. ⛔ A new migration, never an edit: 0036-0042 are applied, and editing one would not re-run it — the source would look fixed while the live policies stayed broken. ⭐ **Two regression tests, enumerated from the live catalogue** (`packages/db/tests/integration/rls.test.ts`): one asserts no policy anywhere matches the raw idiom, so a table added later is covered without anyone remembering; the other proves a no-principal write is refused with `42501` (clean denial) and never `22P02`, on a deliberately `max: 1` pool that forces the connection reuse the bug needs. Both failed first, for the right reason. ⚠️ **Why the existing suite missed this for three tasks:** `rls.test.ts`'s invariant-11 test already exercised the exact scenario — sequential transactions on a pooled connection, then no principal — but asserted against `stores` alone. The invariant was proven for one hand-picked table instead of every table with a policy. That is the actual lesson, and it is why both new tests enumerate. |

| **DEF-079** | ⛔ | **Shareat System** | **`scripts/cutover-purge.ts` cannot run. It `DELETE`s the purge-class tables, and `journal_entries` carries a BEFORE DELETE trigger that raises on any posted row** — *"posted journal entry % cannot be deleted"* (`0003_journal_entries_and_lines.sql`, bible invariant 5). Every real ledger is posted rows, so the purge fails on the first one and the whole transaction rolls back. ⭐ **Proved, not reasoned**: deleting a posted entry in `shareat_test` inside a rolled-back transaction returned the trigger's own message. ⚠️ Nothing caught this because the purge script has no test that runs it against POSTED data — T-119's own tests exercise the classification and the ordering, which are both correct; it is the delete itself that cannot execute. Found 2026-08-29 while building T-134's C2 button, which is exactly the failure the November rehearsal exists to surface | `verified` | ✅ **FIXED same day: `TRUNCATE`, not `DELETE`.** TRUNCATE does not fire row-level DELETE triggers — that is defined behaviour, not a loophole — so the invariant stays fully armed for every ordinary write path while the one operation allowed to empty the ledger can do so. ⭐ Chosen over the alternatives deliberately: a GUC exemption inside the trigger would be *a flag a code path can forget to unset*, and `session_replication_role = 'replica'` disables FK enforcement too, which is far more than this needs. ⚠️ Safe because **every table referencing the ledger is itself purge-class** (verified against `pg_constraint`: ap_payments, ar_charges, ar_collections, ar_write_offs, channel_settlements, expenses, money_transfers, sales_days, trade_orders — none KEEP), so no kept row can be orphaned. | **DEF-342** | ⚠️ | CUSTOMER | ⛔ **A CUSTOMER'S RAW PHONE NUMBER IS USED AS THE FIREBASE AUTH UID, SO THE IDENTITY LIST IS A PLAINTEXT PHONE DIRECTORY.** `src/app/api/customer/sharelebrator/signup/route.ts:80` and `src/app/api/customer/sharelebrator/login/route.ts:53` both call `getAdminAuth().createCustomToken(phone, { loyaltyCustomer: true, phone })` — the first argument is the UID, so the loyalty customer's phone number **becomes the account identifier** in project `shareat-hub-v2`, and is additionally copied into a custom claim. ⛔ **Consequences, in order of seriousness:** (1) **anyone with console or Admin-SDK read access enumerates every loyalty customer's phone number** from the user list alone, with no Firestore read and no audit trail that looks like a data access; (2) the UID is baked into every ID token and every custom claim the client holds, so the number travels further than the record that owns it; (3) ⚠️ **it is effectively permanent** — a Firebase UID cannot be changed, so a customer who changes their number leaves the old one as a live identifier, and honouring a deletion request means deleting the account rather than editing a field. ⭐ **Found 2026-09-13 while establishing which Firebase project ERP v2 signs into** (DEF-340) — read in passing, per RULES §3 *log what you see*, and **not verified against live data**: no user list was enumerated and no phone number was read. v2's terminal design already gets this right (T-304 invariant 2 — *layer 1 creates no `sessions` row*), and this row is the counter-example that shows why that invariant was worth writing. |

Found 2026-09-06 by `ianla-14` with Ian; recorded 2026-09-07 by the orchestrator session, which held this file | `fixed` | ✅ **Restored on the box the same day** (`APP_TIMEZONE=Asia/Manila`, confirmed against `.env.example:13` and `packages/core/src/env.ts:42`); the live file stayed valid through three failed attempts because of the method that follows. ⭐ **Method worth reusing**: build the file in a STAGING copy under `/root`, verify with `grep -c ^KEY` for every key and a value fragment for each, and only then `cp` over the live file. **Rules**: `printf '\n' >> file` before any `cat >>`; `cat -n`, never `nl`, when cross-referencing with `grep -n`. | **DEF-204** | ⚠️ | **Constructing a Drizzle handle silently disarms the shared postgres.js client's jsonb and timestamp handling for every other user of that client.** `drizzle-orm/postgres-js`'s `construct()` mutates the client it is given — `client.options.serializers["114"]` and `["3802"]` become an identity function, as do the parsers AND serializers for `1184`/`1082`/`1083`/`1114` (driver.js:17-22). The mutation is on the shared `options` object, so it reaches the pool and every transaction scoped from it, and it is permanent for that client's lifetime. **Consequence: once `getDb()` has been called anywhere in a process, a raw `getSql()` query using `sql.json()` mis-binds** — the array reaches the wire unserialised and Postgres reports *"The 'string' argument must be of type string… Received an instance of Array"* — **and timestamptz columns read back as raw strings rather than `Date`s.** Neither failure is announced and neither is visible in the calling code. ⭐ **It had already bitten someone and was recorded as a symptom with no cause**: `tests/invariants/accounting-equation.test.ts:55` deliberately avoids the shared `getSql()` cache *"which `sql.json()`'s parameter wrapper does not round-trip through cleanly."* Found 2026-09-07 by T-228, where `createOrganization` must seed the chart of accounts inside the same Drizzle transaction as the org row, which is the first caller that ever needed the seeds to run on a Drizzle-constructed client. ⛔ **The trap is that neither obvious binding works in both worlds**: `sql.json(payload)` is correct on a plain client and throws inside a Drizzle transaction; `${json}::jsonb` — and identically `cast(${json} as jsonb)` — is correct inside a Drizzle transaction and throws 22023 *"cannot call jsonb_to_recordset on a non-array"* on a plain client, because postgres.js reads the first adjacent cast as a type hint, tags the parameter jsonb and re-stringifies it. | `fixed` | **Fixed in `packages/db/seed/chart-of-accounts.ts` and `expense-categories.ts`** by binding the payload as text and casting in SQL: `jsonb_to_recordset((${JSON.stringify(payload)})::text::jsonb)`. `::text` tags the parameter as a type neither client rewrites, so the conversion happens in Postgres and the binding is serializer-INDEPENDENT. Verified in all four combinations against real Postgres, and both directions are covered by tests: `packages/db/tests/integration/chart-of-accounts.test.ts` (77 assertions, plain client) and `packages/domain/tests/integration/organizations.test.ts` (inside a Drizzle transaction). ⛔ **Do not "simplify" it back to either single-cast form** — each looks redundant and each breaks exactly one of the two callers. ⚠️ **Blast radius beyond the fix is NOT swept**: any other raw `getSql()` caller relying on `sql.json()` or on `Date`-typed timestamptz reads is subject to the same mutation. Known `sql.json()` sites today are the two seeds (fixed) and `packages/etl/tests/integration/etl-run.test.ts:547,555,580` (unaffected in practice — that suite uses its own client). The timestamp half has no known victim and was not searched for. |

rather than by a stale constant or a narrow regex. ⭐ **The remedy f2 recorded and the orchestrator endorses: verify a diff line-by-line against the text you actually wrote, never by grepping for an identifier you chose** — and allocate numbers centrally, so two sessions cannot pick the same one to begin with. ⛔ **Do not read this as exonerating the `git add`**: staging a shared file you did not solely author is still what made the loss possible, and explicit-path staging by the other party did not prevent it. Both halves are needed — allocate centrally so the identifier cannot collide, and stage narrowly so a shared file cannot be swept |
